d.title: A compiled graph satisfies the node contract, so it is a node
d.caption: A node is **a callable taking state and returning a partial update** — and a compiled graph is exactly that. So `builder.add_node("clean", inner_graph)` works with no adapter, no wrapper and nothing new to learn, and the inner graph's steps appear in the outer trace. **The same closure property as 1.1's Runnable, one level up**: the composition unit and the composed thing are the same kind of object.

nodes.label: A node: state in, partial update out
And its steps join the outer trace
1.1's closure property, one level up
nodes.sub: unit and composite are one kind

d.title: The explicit wrapper makes the mapping a declared interface
d.caption: Wrapping the inner graph in a function that maps keys in and out is **more code, and the two schemas can now evolve separately** — which is 8.4's input-and-output-schema argument applied to graph composition. **If the inner graph belongs to another team, this is the form you want, because the mapping is a declared interface rather than a coincidence of naming.** Direct nesting couples the two schemas through shared key names that nobody wrote down.

nodes.label: Which is what a team boundary needs

d.title: Five outer checkpoints, and the inner graph's steps are inside one of them
d.caption: The outer run leaves **five checkpoints** and the nested graph's work appears as **one superstep of the parent** — so the inner steps are in the parent's state rather than in their own checkpoint history. Which has a consequence for 9.9's time travel: **you can replay the outer graph from before the nested node, and you cannot resume from the middle of the inner one**, because the parent never recorded a boundary there.

steps.note: the inner graph, in one step

d.title: Three reasons to nest, and two reasons that are not reasons
d.caption: The right-hand column is where the value is. **"This graph is getting long" — a long graph is not a bug**, and nesting to shorten a file buys you a schema boundary you then have to maintain. And **grouping nodes that always run together is already said by a sequence of edges**, so the nesting adds a name and nothing else. Reuse, independent testing and a team boundary are the three that pay.

cells.text: genuinely reused by more than one parent
grouping nodes that always run together
someone else owns the inner graph

d.title: The isolation is one-directional: constrained going in, normal coming out
d.caption: A `Send` gives the worker **its own state**, so it cannot see the parent's other keys or its siblings' work — which is what makes the fan-out safe to reason about. **The worker's return value is merged into the parent state through the parent's reducers**, so the isolation stops at the boundary: **constrained going in, normal coming out.** Which is why §03's reducer requirement is the parent's problem rather than the worker's.

nodes.label: So the reducer is the parent's problem

d.title: The one pattern where 8.3's commonest bug announces itself immediately
d.caption: **Map-reduce *is* N concurrent writes to one key**, so **there is no sequential version of this graph where a missing reducer stays silent.** Everywhere else a missing reducer is latent until a fan-in happens; here the first run raises. Which makes map-reduce the pattern worth building early if you want to understand reducers, because **the framework will not let you misunderstand them.**

nodes.label: Map-reduce is N writes to one key
So it is the pattern to learn on

d.title: The order came out right, and it is not guaranteed
d.caption: The gathered list reads `0:a, 1:b, 2:c, 3:d` — **in order, this time.** 8.3 established why that is luck rather than a property: **updates within a superstep are applied in an order you do not control**, and `operator.add` on lists is not commutative. So **if the order matters, put the index in the value** — which this example does, and which is the only reason the output is readable rather than merely correct.

state: put the index in the value

d.title: The worker has no idea how many siblings it has
d.caption: Nothing bounds the fan-out: a plan with four hundred items produces four hundred workers. **9.3 made the same point from the pattern side — the cap belongs in the orchestrator rather than in the worker, because the worker has no idea how many siblings it has.** Truncating the plan is the crude version; **the considered version rejects the plan and asks for a shorter one, which costs a model call and keeps the failure visible** rather than silently dropping work.

d.title: Five stream modes, and the one to internalise
d.caption: **`updates` is the one worth internalising.** It shows what each node returned keyed by node name, so **when a key has the wrong value it names the node that wrote it in one step, and when a key is missing it shows the absence directly** — which between them cover the two commonest graph bugs in this course. `messages` is per **token** rather than per node, which is what makes a chat UI feel responsive. And `values` has 8.9's off-by-one: it emits the input before any node has run.
cells: the full state after each superstep

cells.text: progress - and it emits the input first
what each node returned, by name
debugging - the only way to see a dropped key
user-facing: per token, not per node

cells: progress from inside a long node

cells.text: the runtime itself - rarely what you want

d.title: Two modes from one call, because running it twice is not equivalent
d.caption: A UI can take `messages` for the text and `updates` for a progress indicator from **one** call. Which matters for a sharper reason than efficiency: **running the graph twice is not merely wasteful — a graph with side effects or a checkpointer cannot be run twice equivalently.** The second run resumes from the first's checkpoint, so it is not a repeat, it is a continuation.

nodes.label: Running twice is not equivalent
nodes.sub: with side effects or a checkpointer

nodes.label: The second run continues the first

d.title: custom is the only way a long node reports anything
d.caption: Every other mode emits **at a node boundary**, so a node that takes thirty seconds is silent for thirty seconds — `updates` fires once, when it finishes. The stream writer emits from **inside**, so `step 1 of 3`, `step 2 of 3`, `step 3 of 3` arrive while the node is still running. Which is the gap in the other four modes rather than a convenience: **node granularity is the wrong granularity for a slow node.**

d.title: Five situations, and the mode each one wants
d.caption: Read as a lookup. The first row is two modes rather than one, which §03 showed costs nothing. The fourth carries its own warning — **`values` for a progress bar, remembering the off-by-one**, or the bar starts at one step of progress that has not happened. And the last row is honest about `debug`: it exists for understanding the runtime, **which is rarely what an application wants.**

d.title: The default retries connection errors and 5xx, and it is a function you can read
d.caption: `default_retry_on` is ordinary code: **`ConnectionError` yes, an HTTP status error only when 500 ≤ status < 600**, and so on. Which is worth reading rather than assuming, because it settles the question 2.6 raised from the other side: **the default does not retry a 400, a 401 or a validation error** — so the dangerous case is not the default being too broad, it is **a custom `retry_on` written more broadly than the default.**

nodes.label: So not 400, 401 or a validation error
The risk is a broader custom policy

d.title: Writing the retryable set down makes the decision reviewable
d.caption: `retry_on=(RuntimeError,)` and the node succeeds on **attempt 3**, having run its body **three times.** Which is usually what you want — **the set of retryable errors for your dependencies is knowable and short, and writing it down makes the decision reviewable instead of inherited.** An inherited default is a decision nobody made; a tuple in the source is one somebody can disagree with in a pull request.

d.title: A retry policy is not an error-handling strategy on its own
d.caption: **It only buys you another chance at the same thing.** Something still has to decide **what exhaustion means** — route to a fallback, hand the failure to the model to react to (which 9.2's `ToolNode` does), or fail the request. A graph with retries and no answer to that question **has moved the failure later rather than handled it**, and the symptom is a request that takes three times as long before failing identically.

nodes.label: A retry policy
nodes.sub: another chance at the same thing

nodes.label: Or hand it to the model
No answer: 3x the latency, same failure

d.title: Two side effects for one successful run
d.caption: **The retried node re-runs from the top**, so a node whose first statement has a side effect performs it on every attempt: **the run succeeded once and recorded two side effects.** Which is 9.7's re-execution constraint arriving for the third time in this course — interrupt, fork, and now retry — and the same remedy applies: **put the effect after whatever can fail, or make it idempotent.**

steps.code: the third time in this course

d.title: There is no timeout= on add_node
d.caption: So the options are **the client's own timeout inside the node**, a wrapper around the node body, or **the caller's timeout around `invoke()`** — and they are not equivalent. A client timeout fails one call and lets the retry policy see it. A caller timeout around `invoke()` kills the whole run, **including the checkpoint write**, so a graph that times out at the top may leave no record of how far it got.

nodes.label: Fails one call; retry sees it
Kills the run, checkpoint write included

d.title: Budget exhausted is a state you can route on
d.caption: Counting in state and checking in the router gives the loop a bound **you own** — and that is 8.9's whole argument: **success and runaway become distinguishable, and "budget exhausted" is a state you can route on, record and return to the caller** rather than an exception that looks identical to an infinite loop. The `recursion_limit` raises the same error for a working graph that needed one more step and for a graph that will never stop.

d.title: A counter bounds iterations; it does not notice a loop making no progress
d.caption: The two guards catch different things. **A budget stops a loop that never exits. A progress check stops a loop that exits and achieves nothing** — iterating five times and producing the same value each time passes the budget and wastes all of it. Keeping the previous value **needs a state key, which is a legitimate use of state rather than the smell 8.8 warned about**: the comparison is genuinely a property of the run rather than something a node already knew.

d.title: The fan-in that is not a deadlock
d.caption: A conditional edge that takes one of two branches leaves the join node with **one incoming path satisfied and one never taken** — and the graph does **not** hang. 8.6's rule is about **paths the runtime will execute**, not edges drawn on the diagram, so a skipped branch is not a pending dependency. Which is why the guard here is a **partial-input check in the fan-in node**: the node runs, and it has to cope with a key no branch wrote.

nodes.label: The join has two incoming edges
It does NOT hang
nodes.sub: a skipped branch is not pending

d.title: Five guards, and each belongs somewhere specific
d.caption: The *where* column is the content. **Both loop guards belong in the router**, because that is where a routing decision can be made; a check inside a node can only raise. The **partial-input check belongs in the fan-in node**, because that is the only place that knows a branch was skipped. And `recursion_limit` is **a backstop rather than a guard** — it catches everything the other four missed, including what you did not predict.
cells: a loop that exits achieving nothing

d.title: A node is a function, so the first level of testing needs no graph
d.caption: A node takes a dict and returns a dict. **So testing one is calling it with a dict and asserting on the dict that comes back** — no graph, no compile, no checkpointer, no model. Which makes the cheapest tests in this module the ones people skip, because the function looks too simple to be worth a test. It is also the level that catches 8.2's silent drop and 8.5's whole-state return, both of which are visible in the returned dict alone.

nodes.label: So call it with a dict
Skipped because it looks too simple
nodes.sub: which is why these bugs ship

d.title: The router is a pure function, and covering every outcome costs almost nothing
d.caption: **The failure it prevents is 8.7's**: a router returning a key the path map lacks **compiles fine and fails at runtime on one branch only.** Since the router is a pure function of state, **covering every outcome costs almost nothing — and it is skipped precisely because it looks too trivial to write.** Which pairs with §01: the two cheapest test levels in the module are the two most often absent.

nodes.label: And fails on one branch only

d.title: Two tests passed and re-invoking one thread shows why that was luck
d.caption: `test_a` and `test_b` both produce `['double', 'small']` — and **re-invoking test_a's thread gives `['double', 'small', 'double', 'small']`**, because 9.4's checkpointer continued from the persisted state. Which is the trap in testing anything stateful: **a per-test `thread_id` is not optional.** Two tests sharing one thread pass individually and interfere when the suite order changes, which is the hardest class of flaky test to diagnose.

steps.note: a per-test thread_id is not optional

d.title: Mocking the graph tests the mock
d.caption: Script the model and **everything else stays real — the graph, the reducers, the tool node, the checkpointer.** The alternative is the point: **mocking the graph or patching node functions tests the mock. It would have passed in every one of the three failures above, because the mock has no schema to drop a key against and no reducer to be missing.** Which is 4.8's argument in a graph setting: replace the one non-deterministic component and the rest becomes assertable.

nodes.label: No schema to drop a key against
nodes.sub: and no reducer to be missing

nodes.label: So it passes all three failures

d.title: Five assertions, and the one that catches prompt bugs
d.caption: **`model.seen` — asserting on what the model actually received — is the one that catches prompt and history bugs**, which is 4.8's finding that testing the input is where the cheap bugs are. The other four cover the graph's own failure modes: dropped keys and bad reducers in the final state, routing bugs in the visited sequence, loops in the call count, and the pause itself in `get_state().next`.

items.label: What the model received
